notes.definition: Plant tissues are groups of similar cells with structures adapted to their functions. They include epidermal tissue, palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll, xylem, phloem and meristem tissue. The leaf is a plant organ made of several of these tissues, with guard cells surrounding the stomata.
explanation: The leaf is a plant organ: it contains several tissues working together to carry out photosynthesis and gas exchange. Its main tissues, from top to bottom, are the upper epidermis, palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll and lower epidermis, with xylem and phloem running through it in veins (vascular bundles). Guard cells surround the stomata, which are found mainly in the lower epidermis.

Epidermal tissue covers the upper and lower surfaces of the leaf. The upper epidermis is a single layer of transparent cells, so light passes through to the cells below. Epidermal cells secrete a waxy cuticle, which is waterproof and reduces water loss by evaporation. The lower epidermis contains most of the stomata, so fewer stomata are exposed to direct sunlight and less water is lost.

Palisade mesophyll is where most photosynthesis happens. Its cells are tall and tightly packed near the top of the leaf, where they receive the most light, and they contain many chloroplasts to absorb light. Spongy mesophyll lies below. Its cells are loosely packed with large air spaces between them, giving a large surface area for gases (carbon dioxide, oxygen and water vapour) to diffuse in and out of cells.

Xylem tissue transports water and dissolved mineral ions from the roots up to the stem and leaves. Xylem is made of dead cells forming hollow tubes strengthened by lignin, which also supports the plant. Phloem tissue transports dissolved sugars made in photosynthesis from the leaves to the rest of the plant, for immediate use or storage. Phloem is made of elongated living cells with pores in their end walls (sieve plates) that let cell sap move from one cell to the next.

Meristem tissue is found at the growing tips of shoots and roots. Its cells divide rapidly by mitosis and can differentiate into many different types of plant cell, allowing the plant to grow throughout its life. Guard cells are a pair of specialised cells around each stoma. When the plant has plenty of water, the guard cells become turgid and the stoma opens, allowing gas exchange; when water is short, they become flaccid and the stoma closes, reducing water loss.
keyFacts: The leaf is a plant organ.
Upper epidermis: transparent, lets light through; covered with a waxy cuticle to reduce water loss.
Palisade mesophyll: tightly packed cells with many chloroplasts near the upper surface for photosynthesis.
Spongy mesophyll: loosely packed cells with air spaces for gas diffusion.
Xylem: hollow tubes of dead cells strengthened by lignin; carry water and mineral ions upwards.
Phloem: elongated living cells with pores in end walls; carry dissolved sugars around the plant.
Meristem tissue at shoot and root tips divides and can differentiate into different cell types.
Guard cells surround stomata and control gas exchange and water loss.
Most stomata are in the lower epidermis.

keyTerms.definition: The outer layer of cells covering the upper and lower surfaces of a leaf.
A waterproof layer on the epidermis that reduces water loss.
A layer of tightly packed cells with many chloroplasts where most photosynthesis occurs.
Loosely packed leaf cells with air spaces that allow gases to diffuse.
Tissue of hollow tubes strengthened by lignin that transports water and mineral ions from the roots.
Tissue of elongated cells with pores in the end walls that transports dissolved sugars.
Tissue at the growing tips of shoots and roots whose cells divide and can differentiate into different cell types.
A pore in the leaf surface that allows gases to diffuse in and out.
A pair of cells around a stoma that change shape to open and close it.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think xylem carries sugars and phloem carries water.
misconceptions.right: In fact xylem carries water and mineral ions; phloem carries dissolved sugars.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think stomata are mainly on the upper surface of the leaf.
misconceptions.right: In fact most stomata are on the lower surface, which is cooler and shaded, so less water is lost.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think xylem is made of living cells.
misconceptions.right: In fact xylem is made of dead cells that form hollow tubes strengthened with lignin; phloem cells are living.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the upper epidermis carries out most photosynthesis.
misconceptions.right: In fact the epidermis is transparent and has few chloroplasts; most photosynthesis happens in the palisade mesophyll.

realWorld: Gardeners take cuttings from shoot tips because meristem tissue can produce new roots and shoots, giving clones of a plant.
Plants from dry habitats often have a thick waxy cuticle and fewer stomata to reduce water loss.
Lignin in xylem makes wood strong enough to be used as a building material.
examTips: Learn the order of leaf layers from top to bottom: cuticle, upper epidermis, palisade, spongy, lower epidermis (with guard cells and stomata).
Always link structure to function, for example 'many chloroplasts, so more light is absorbed for photosynthesis'.
Remember: xylem is dead with lignin and carries water; phloem is living with pores in end walls and carries sugars.
For guard cells say turgid means open and flaccid means closed.
summary: The leaf is an organ made of several plant tissues.
Epidermis is transparent with a waxy cuticle to reduce water loss.
Palisade mesophyll has many chloroplasts; spongy mesophyll has air spaces.
Xylem carries water and ions; phloem carries dissolved sugars.
Meristem tissue at shoot and root tips divides and differentiates.
Guard cells open and close stomata to control gas exchange and water loss.

questions.question: Which tissue in the leaf carries out most photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: Palisade cells have the most chloroplasts and are near the top of the leaf.

questions.question: What does xylem transport?
questions.explanation: Xylem carries water and mineral ions from the roots; phloem carries dissolved sugars.

questions.question: Where is meristem tissue found?
options: At the growing tips of shoots and roots
questions.explanation: Meristems are at the tips of shoots and roots, where growth occurs.

questions.question: What is the function of the waxy cuticle?
questions.explanation: The waxy layer is waterproof, so less water evaporates from the leaf surface.

questions.question: Which feature of spongy mesophyll is an adaptation for gas exchange?
questions.explanation: Air spaces allow carbon dioxide, oxygen and water vapour to diffuse between cells and stomata.

questions.question: Which statement about phloem is correct?
options: It is made of dead cells strengthened by lignin
It transports water from the roots
It is made of elongated cells with pores in the end walls
It is found only in roots
questions.explanation: Phloem cells are living and have sieve plates (pores) in their end walls. Lignin and water transport describe xylem.

questions.question: Why is the upper epidermis transparent?
options: To allow light to pass through to the palisade cells
To allow carbon dioxide to enter
questions.explanation: Light must reach the chloroplasts in the palisade layer.

questions.question: What happens to guard cells when a plant is short of water?
options: They become turgid and the stoma opens
They become flaccid and the stoma closes
They become turgid and the stoma closes
They divide to make new stomata
questions.explanation: Guard cells lose water and become flaccid, closing the stoma and reducing further water loss.

questions.question: Why are most stomata found on the lower surface of a leaf?
options: The lower surface receives more light
The lower surface is cooler and shaded, so less water evaporates
Carbon dioxide only enters from below
The cuticle is thicker on the lower surface
questions.explanation: Having stomata away from direct sunlight reduces water loss while still allowing gas exchange.

questions.question: Why is xylem made of dead cells with no end walls?
options: To form continuous hollow tubes so water can flow freely
questions.explanation: Without cell contents or end walls, xylem forms an unobstructed tube for the transpiration stream.

questions.question: Which tissue contains cells that can differentiate into any type of plant cell?
questions.explanation: Meristem cells are undifferentiated and can become many cell types.

questions.question: A student counts 45 stomata in an area of 0.2 mm². Calculate the number of stomata per mm².
questions.explanation: Density = number ÷ area = 45 ÷ 0.2 = 225 per mm².

questions.question: A palisade cell is 75 μm long. In a drawing it is 30 mm long. Calculate the magnification of the drawing.

The field of view of a microscope is a circle of diameter 0.4 mm. A student counts 22 stomata in it. Calculate the number of stomata per mm². Use π = 3.14 and give your answer to the nearest whole number.
questions.explanation: Area = πr² with r = 0.2 mm, giving 0.1256 mm². 22 ÷ 0.1256 = 175.2, which is 175 to the nearest whole number. Using the diameter instead of the radius gives an area four times too large.

questions.question: On the lower surface of a leaf there were 280 stomata per mm². On the upper surface there were 35 per mm². Calculate the percentage of the stomata (in 1 mm² of each surface) that were on the lower surface.
A palisade cell contains 48 chloroplasts. A spongy mesophyll cell contains 15 chloroplasts. Calculate how many times more chloroplasts the palisade cell has.
questions.explanation: 48 ÷ 15 = 3.2 times more, reflecting the palisade layer's role as the main site of photosynthesis.

questions.question: Name the tissue that transports dissolved sugars in a plant.
questions.explanation: Phloem carries sugars made in the leaves.

questions.question: Give two ways palisade mesophyll cells are adapted for photosynthesis.
markScheme: 1 mark: many chloroplasts to absorb light
1 mark: tightly packed / near the upper surface to receive most light
questions.explanation: Both adaptations increase the amount of light absorbed.

questions.question: Explain how xylem is adapted for its function.
markScheme: 1 mark: hollow tubes of dead cells with no end walls, so water flows freely
1 mark: walls strengthened by lignin to withstand pressure / support the plant
questions.explanation: Each structural feature is linked to water transport or support.

questions.question: Explain why the leaf is described as an organ.
markScheme: 1 mark: it is made of several different tissues (for example epidermis, mesophyll, xylem, phloem)
1 mark: that work together to perform a function such as photosynthesis
questions.explanation: An organ contains different tissues working together.

questions.question: Describe how guard cells control the opening and closing of stomata, and why this is important.
markScheme: 1 mark: when guard cells take in water they become turgid and the stoma opens
1 mark: when they lose water they become flaccid and the stoma closes
1 mark: this balances gas exchange (carbon dioxide in for photosynthesis) with reducing water loss
questions.explanation: The plant needs carbon dioxide but must also conserve water.

questions.question: Explain how the structure of the spongy mesophyll and the stomata together allow carbon dioxide to reach the palisade cells.
markScheme: 1 mark: carbon dioxide diffuses into the leaf through open stomata
1 mark: it diffuses through the air spaces in the spongy mesophyll, which give a large surface area
1 mark: down a concentration gradient (maintained because palisade cells use carbon dioxide in photosynthesis)
questions.explanation: The answer links the gas pathway to the structures and to diffusion.

questions.question: A plant species that lives in a desert has a very thick waxy cuticle and its stomata are sunk into pits. Suggest how these features help it survive.
markScheme: 1 mark: thick cuticle reduces evaporation from the leaf surface
1 mark: sunken stomata trap moist air, reducing the concentration gradient so less water vapour diffuses out
questions.explanation: Both features reduce water loss in a hot, dry habitat.

questions.question: Name the substance that strengthens the walls of xylem.
questions.explanation: Lignin makes xylem rigid and helps support the plant.

questions.question: Describe the tissues found in a leaf and give the function of each.
markScheme: Indicative content: waxy cuticle reduces water loss; upper epidermis transparent, lets light through, protects; palisade mesophyll many chloroplasts, main site of photosynthesis; spongy mesophyll air spaces for gas exchange, some photosynthesis; xylem transports water and mineral ions to the leaf; phloem transports sugars away from the leaf; lower epidermis contains stomata; guard cells open and close stomata to control gas exchange and water loss.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): at least four tissues described with correct functions, in a logical order.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): a few tissues named, with limited or partly incorrect functions.
questions.explanation: Work from the top of the leaf to the bottom so you do not miss any tissue.

questions.question: Compare the structure and function of xylem and phloem, and explain how the tissues in a leaf are arranged to maximise photosynthesis while limiting water loss.
markScheme: Indicative content: xylem: dead cells, hollow tubes, no end walls, lignin strengthens; transports water and mineral ions upwards from roots; one direction. Phloem: living elongated cells with pores in end walls; transports dissolved sugars from leaves to rest of plant for use or storage. Leaf arrangement: transparent upper epidermis lets light through; palisade cells near top packed with chloroplasts; spongy mesophyll air spaces for carbon dioxide diffusion; xylem brings water for photosynthesis; phloem removes sugars; waxy cuticle reduces evaporation; stomata mainly on lower surface; guard cells close stomata when water is short.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): clear direct comparison of xylem and phloem plus well-linked explanation of leaf arrangement for both photosynthesis and water conservation.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): some comparison of xylem and phloem and some leaf adaptations.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): basic facts about either tissue or leaf features with little explanation.
questions.explanation: Use comparative words for xylem and phloem, then explain the trade-off between letting carbon dioxide in and keeping water in.
